questions.topic: The electorate Article One points to for House votes
questions.learningObjective: state whose qualifications Article One makes the measure of the House electorate
questions.stem: Article One, Section 2 says who votes for a Representative, and it does it by pointing at a state office. What does it point at?

options.text: At the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the state legislature
At the qualifications the state constitution sets for the most numerous branch of its legislature
options.misconception: confuses the office the rule points at with the document that defines the office

options.text: At the qualifications a state sets for the electorate of its own executive officers
options.misconception: points the rule at the wrong state office

options.text: At a national qualification, since the Constitution sets the standard for every federal election
options.misconception: assumes the Constitution supplies the voting qualification itself

questions.explanation: The clause provides that the House shall be composed of members chosen every second year by the people of the several states, and that the Electors in each State shall have the Qualifications requisite for Electors of the most numerous Branch of the State Legislature. So the standard is not in the Constitution at all; it is a pointer into each state's law, and the pointer aims at the electorate of the largest of the state's two legislative chambers. That is why the second answer is a near miss, since a state constitution is where such a qualification usually sits, but the words say most numerous branch and not the document. The Seventeenth Amendment used the same pointer for senatorial electors, which is what makes the two electorates normally coincide.
questions.hint: Find the words that describe the qualifications and ask what office they belong to.

options.misconception: uses the qualifications for a senator in place of those for a representative

options.text: Attained twenty-five years, been nine years a citizen, and be an inhabitant of the state when chosen

options.text: Attained thirty years, been seven years a citizen, and be an inhabitant of the state when chosen

options.text: Attained twenty-five years, been seven years a citizen, and be an inhabitant of the state when chosen

questions.explanation: The clause provides that no person shall be a Representative who shall not have attained to the age of twenty-five years, and been seven years a citizen of the United States, and who shall not, when elected, be an inhabitant of that state in which he shall be chosen. options.misconception: reverses the two prepositions and so swaps the two clauses

options.text: A Representative must be an inhabitant of that state in which he shall be chosen, and a senator of that state for which he shall be chosen
Both clauses use the same words, so the residency requirements are identical in form
options.misconception: overlooks the difference between in which and for which

options.text: A Representative must be an inhabitant of the state, and a senator must be an inhabitant of the district
options.misconception: introduces a district requirement the text does not contain

The Senate clause reads who shall not, when elected, be an Inhabitant of that State for which he shall be chosen. The only difference is the pair of words in which and for which, and it is the kind of difference that disappears when a clause is paraphrased, which is why the second answer is the one students reach for. questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The people counted in the original apportionment
questions.learningObjective: identify what the original apportionment rule counted and what it excluded

stimulus.body: Article One, Section 2, Clause 3 provides that representatives and direct taxes shall be apportioned according to the respective numbers of the states, which shall be determined by adding to the whole number of free persons, including those bound to service for a term of years, and excluding Indians not taxed, three fifths of all other persons.

questions.stem: The source quotes the original apportionment rule. Which three of the following are part of how the number for a state was determined?

options.text: The whole number of free persons in the state
Those bound to service for a term of years, counted in full
Three fifths of all persons not already counted in full
Indians not taxed, counted in the same way as free persons
options.misconception: believes the excluded group was actually included in the count

questions.explanation: The clause builds the number in three steps and names one exclusion. It adds the whole number of free persons, and in doing so it includes those bound to service for a term of years in the same full count, which is why the first and second choices are both right. It then excludes Indians not taxed, and only after that does it add three fifths of all other persons, so the third choice is right as well. The fourth choice is the error of reading the exclusion as an inclusion, and it is worth pausing on, because the excluded group was the one most often overlooked in the whole clause. A count of three that left out the free persons, or that counted the excluded group, would not be the count the clause specifies.
questions.hint: Follow the three verbs the clause uses, and then find the one group it takes out.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The three-fifths count worked out
questions.learningObjective: compute a state's original apportionment number and the one the Fourteenth Amendment substituted

stimulus.body: A state contains 400,000 people in all: 250,000 free persons, 100,000 persons bound to service for a term of years, 40,000 enslaved persons, and 10,000 Indians not taxed.

questions.stem: Using the original rule, how many persons does the state count for apportionment, and how many would it count under the rule in section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment?

options.text: 350,000 under the original rule and 390,000 under the Fourteenth Amendment
options.misconception: leaves out the three-fifths addition for the persons not counted in full

options.text: 390,000 under the original rule and 374,000 under the Fourteenth Amendment
options.misconception: reverses which rule produces which figure

options.text: 374,000 under both rules, because the excluded group was counted under each
options.misconception: believes the two rules produce the same number for this state

options.text: 374,000 under the original rule and 390,000 under the Fourteenth Amendment

questions.explanation: Under the original rule the state counts the free persons in full, which is 250,000, and the persons bound to service for a term of years in full, which is 100,000, and then three fifths of everyone left, which is three fifths of 40,000, or 24,000. The Indians not taxed are excluded, so the total is 250,000 plus 100,000 plus 24,000, which is 374,000. Under section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment the state counts the whole number of persons in it, excluding Indians not taxed, which is 400,000 less 10,000, so 390,000. The amendment therefore added 16,000 to this state's count, and the first wrong answer stops at 350,000 by omitting the three-fifths step entirely.
questions.hint: Do the original count in the three steps the clause names, then take the whole number less the excluded group.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The ratio that caps a state's representation
questions.learningObjective: apply the cap on the number of Representatives to a state's count
questions.stem: Article One, Section 2 says the number of Representatives shall not exceed one for every thirty thousand, but each state shall have at least one Representative. A state's count for apportionment is 174,000. At most how many Representatives may it have under that rule?

options.text: One, because the rule fixes the number at one and forbids a state from having more
options.misconception: reads the floor of one as though it were also the ceiling

options.text: Five and four fifths, because the rule fixes the number at the exact ratio
options.misconception: treats a ceiling as though it required a fractional number of seats

options.text: Five, because six would require a count of 180,000 and the state has less than that
Six, because 174,000 is more than five multiples of thirty thousand
options.misconception: rounds the ratio up instead of treating the rule as a ceiling

questions.explanation: The rule is a ceiling, not a formula that produces a seat count. Six Representatives on this state's count would be a ratio of one for every 29,000, since six times thirty thousand is 180,000 and the state has 174,000, and a ratio better than one for every thirty thousand is what the clause forbids. Five Representatives is one for every 34,800, which is within the ceiling, so five is the largest whole number the rule allows. The second answer is the error the word exceed is there to prevent, since it rounds the ratio up; the third confuses the floor of one with the ceiling; and the fourth treats the ratio as though it fixed a number exactly, which no legislature can do.
questions.hint: Multiply by the ratio and ask whether the next whole number would break the ceiling.

questions.topic: The original allotment of seats to thirteen states
questions.learningObjective: add the original allotment of Representatives across the thirteen states

stimulus.body: Article One, Section 2, Clause 3 lists the states that existed when the Constitution was adopted and the number of Representatives each was entitled to choose until an enumeration should be made: New Hampshire three, Massachusetts eight, Rhode Island and Providence Plantations one, Connecticut five, New York six, New Jersey four, Pennsylvania eight, Delaware one, Maryland six, Virginia ten, North Carolina five, South Carolina five, and Georgia three.

options.text: Sixty-three, because the three seats for New Hampshire and for Georgia are each read as two
options.misconception: reads two entries one lower than the text gives them

options.text: Sixty-five, the sum of the thirteen entries
Sixty-six, because Rhode Island and Providence Plantations counts as two states
options.misconception: splits one entry containing two names into two states

options.text: Sixty-four, because the entry for Massachusetts is eight and is counted as seven
options.misconception: reads one entry one lower than the text gives it

Running the sum: three plus eight is eleven, plus one is twelve, plus five is seventeen, plus six is twenty-three, plus four is twenty-seven, plus eight is thirty-five, plus one is thirty-six, plus six is forty-two, plus ten is fifty-two, plus five is fifty-seven, plus five is sixty-two, plus three is sixty-five. questions.topic: How often the enumeration must be taken
questions.learningObjective: state the two intervals the census clause requires

Within one year after the first meeting of the Congress, and within every subsequent term of ten years

options.misconception: believes the clause leaves the timing to a state's request

questions.topic: Who issues a writ for a House vacancy
questions.learningObjective: identify who issues the writ of election that fills a House vacancy
questions.stem: A Representative's seat falls vacant. Article One, Section 2 says who issues the writ that fills it. Who is that?

options.text: The Congress, by a statute directing the Secretary of State to issue it
options.misconception: moves the writ from the state to the national legislature

options.text: The legislature of the state, by its own resolution
options.misconception: confuses the body that prescribes the manner with the authority that issues the writ

options.text: The people of the state, at a special election called without any writ
options.misconception: assumes an election can be called without the writ the clause requires

options.text: The executive authority of the state in which the vacancy occurred

The operative words are the executive authority thereof, which points to the state rather than to the national government, and shall issue Writs of Election, which makes the writ the formal step that sets the election in motion. The third answer is the most attractive because the same section makes the state legislature the body that prescribes the manner of holding elections, but prescribing the manner and issuing the writ are two different acts assigned to two different authorities. questions.topic: The one vote each senator has
questions.learningObjective: state what Article One says about the vote of a senator
questions.stem: The opening sentence of Article One, Section 3 ends with a provision about voting. What does it say?

options.text: That each senator shall have one vote, except in the last year of a term
options.misconception: invents a term-based exception the clause does not contain

options.text: That each senator shall have one vote, which the Seventeenth Amendment replaced
options.misconception: believes the direct-election amendment changed the vote rule

options.text: That each senator shall have one vote, which the Seventeenth Amendment left as it stood
That each senator shall have two votes whenever the chamber is equally divided
options.misconception: gives a senator a weighted vote in a tie

The Seventeenth Amendment rewrote the opening of that sentence to read elected by the people thereof in place of chosen by the Legislature thereof, and left the words for six years and each Senator shall have one vote exactly as they were, which is what makes the fourth answer wrong. The second answer confuses the senator's single vote with the tie-breaking role the next clause gives the Vice President, who has no vote unless the chamber is equally divided.

questions.topic: Dividing the Senate into three classes
questions.learningObjective: compute the class sizes when Senate seats are divided as equally as may be

stimulus.body: A state has two senators, as the Constitution requires. Across the whole chamber there are 100 seats, and the clause requires the senators to be divided as equally as may be into three classes.

questions.stem: With 100 seats divided as equally as may be into three classes, what are the sizes of the three classes?

options.text: Thirty-three and thirty-four and thirty-three, with the remainder in the first class
options.misconception: places the remainder in the wrong class of the three

options.text: Thirty-four, thirty-three and thirty-three, because one hundred leaves a remainder of one
Thirty-three, thirty-three and thirty-three, because a hundred divides evenly by three
options.misconception: supposes a division with no remainder and loses a seat

options.text: Fifty, fifty and nil, because the seats are divided between two classes instead of three
options.misconception: divides the chamber into the wrong number of classes

questions.explanation: Divide one hundred by three and the quotient is thirty-three with a remainder of one, because three times thirty-three is ninety-nine. So the classes cannot all be thirty-three without losing a seat, and they cannot be thirty-four each because that would be a hundred and two. The clause says the senators shall be divided as equally as may be, which is a rule about the smallest gap between classes rather than about equal size, so the sizes are thirty-four, thirty-three and thirty-three, differing by one. The last answer has the same three numbers as the correct one and is therefore a different statement about which class is the larger, and a question about the sequence of classes is not answered by the numbers alone.
questions.hint: Divide, keep the remainder, and check that the sizes differ by no more than one.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The temporary appointment sentence in Section 3
questions.learningObjective: explain how the temporary-appointment sentence in Article One, Section 3 fits with the Seventeenth Amendment
questions.stem: Article One, Section 3 still prints a sentence about a state's executive making temporary appointments when a senatorial vacancy happens during the recess of the state legislature. How does that sentence stand with the Seventeenth Amendment?

options.text: The amendment keeps the writ of election as the rule and lets a legislature empower its executive to make temporary appointments, so the sentence survives in substance
The amendment struck the sentence out of the text, so the printed words have no effect whatever
options.misconception: believes the amendment removed the printed sentence rather than adding a proviso

options.text: The amendment replaced the executive with the state legislature, so a vacancy is now filled by appointment of the legislature
options.misconception: turns the temporary appointment into a permanent legislative appointment

options.text: The amendment made temporary appointments unnecessary, because only an elected senator may now serve
options.misconception: reads the direct-election requirement as a bar on any temporary appointment

questions.explanation: Two texts have to be read together. The printed clause says that if vacancies happen by resignation or otherwise during the recess of the legislature of any state, the executive thereof may make temporary appointments until the next meeting of the legislature, which shall then fill such vacancies. The Seventeenth Amendment provides that when vacancies happen in the representation of any state in the Senate the executive authority of that state shall issue writs of election, and adds that the legislature of any state may empower the executive to make temporary appointments until the people fill the vacancies by election. So the amendment made the writ of election the rule and preserved the temporary appointment as a state option, which is why the second and fourth answers are wrong. The third answer mistakes a temporary appointment for a permanent one.
questions.hint: Read the amendment's proviso and ask what it allows a state legislature to authorise.

questions.topic: The Vice President as President of the Senate
questions.learningObjective: state when the Vice President has a vote in the Senate
questions.stem: Article One, Section 3 makes the Vice President the President of the Senate and then limits the vote. What is the limit?

options.text: The Vice President has no vote at any time, because the clause says no vote without exception
options.misconception: drops the exception the clause states in the same sentence

options.text: The Vice President has a vote whenever a question is called, but no vote on a bill
options.misconception: invents a subject-matter exception the clause does not contain

options.text: The Vice President has a vote only while acting as President of the United States
options.misconception: attaches the vote to the wrong office entirely

So the presiding officer of the chamber is a non-voting member in ordinary business, and the single exception is a tie. The exception is enough to do the work because a tied vote cannot carry a question and a casting vote breaks it, which is the whole reason the exception exists. The second answer reads the sentence as though it stopped at no vote, and the third and fourth answers add exceptions or move the vote to another office, none of which the clause mentions. The clause's own pronoun is plural, which is a reminder that its words are old.
questions.hint: Read the words that follow the comma after no Vote.

questions.learningObjective: state the limit Article One places on the judgment in an impeachment

options.text: It may extend to removal and to the death of the convicted person, and nothing else

questions.topic: Who the Elections Clause makes the default rulemaker

questions.stem: The Elections Clause says the times, places and manner of holding elections shall be prescribed in each state by the legislature thereof. Explain why the choice of that word has been the subject of disagreement, and be clear about what the text settles and what it does not.

answer.exemplar: The clause names one actor, the legislature of the state, and says nothing about anyone else, so the text does settle who exercises the power on its face. The disagreement is about whether naming the legislature excludes the rest of the state. One view reads the naming as a grant, so the legislature is the body the Constitution chooses to make the rules and no other body may make them instead. The other view reads it as a default, so that the legislature speaks for the state and a rule the state has adopted by some other route, including at a referendum, is a rule of the state just as much. The reason the question keeps arising is structural rather than textual: the clause does not say the legislature has exclusive power, and it does not say anyone else has any, so the text is silent on the point that is being argued about it. A strong answer should also note what is not in dispute. The time of an election is a federal interest because the same section lets Congress set when the Congress meets, and Congress's power to make and alter regulations is in the same sentence, so nothing in the disagreement touches the one subject the clause excepts from Congress's power, which is the places of choosing senators. An answer that picks a side without addressing the default reading has skipped the part of the question that makes it hard, and an answer that says the clause is silent about everything is wrong, because it is explicit about the legislature.

questions.explanation: A strong answer states the two readings of the word legislature, identifies that the clause neither grants exclusively nor excludes anyone, and marks the subjects that are settled by the same sentence. It should not attribute the disagreement to any particular decision or to any recent practice.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause says the legislature has exclusive power, and whether it says anyone else has none.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What a chamber's rules may not do
questions.learningObjective: explain the source of the limit on a chamber's power to determine its own rules
questions.stem: Article One, Section 5 says that each house may determine the rules of its proceedings. A chamber adopts a rule providing that a bill shall be considered without objection from any member who is absent. Explain where the limit on such a rule comes from, and why the clause does not itself supply one.

answer.exemplar: The clause is a grant of power to each house and the limit on that power is not in the clause, which is the point of the question. Article One, Section 5 provides that each House may determine the Rules of its Proceedings, punish its Members for disorderly Behaviour, and, with the concurrence of two thirds, expel a Member, and it does not attach a standard to the first of those powers. A rule is therefore a legislative act whose authority comes from the clause, and the clause's own words supply no test for judging one. The limit comes from outside, and there are two directions from which it arrives. The Constitution binds the chamber whether or not the rule acknowledges it, so a rule cannot treat as constitutional something the Constitution does not establish, and cannot dispense with a constitutional requirement. And the same section contains a rule about the chamber that a later rule cannot override, because the section says the yeas and nays on any question shall at the desire of one fifth of those present be entered on the Journal, which is a constraint the chamber's own rulemaking power does not reach. The second direction is the more useful one for a concrete example, because the journal clause is a command about what must be recorded rather than a matter of chamber convenience. A strong answer should say that the limit is external, identify at least one external source, and avoid claiming that the clause itself limits the rulemaking power, which it does not do.

questions.explanation: A strong answer says that the limit comes from outside the rulemaking clause, names the Constitution as binding the chamber whether or not a rule accepts it, and points to a specific command in the same section that a chamber rule cannot override. It should not claim the clause limits its own grant, because it does not.
questions.hint: Ask what else in the Constitution commands the chamber, and whether a rule can set that aside.

Two features of the drafting are worth holding on to. It names the first and fourth clauses of the ninth section of the first article, and the first of those is the clause on the migration or importation of persons and the fourth is the clause requiring a direct tax to be laid in proportion to the census, so the pair is a set of clauses about two politically charged subjects. And the protection is tied to a year and to amendments made before it, so the proviso's own terms were spent at that year and the clauses it protected became amendable in the ordinary way, which is what happened to the first of them when the Thirteenth Amendment dealt with the subject in an entirely different way.
questions.hint: Read the proviso's words and write down the section and the two clause numbers.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The two provisos in Article Five
questions.learningObjective: count and identify the two protections written as provisos in Article Five

stimulus.body: Article Five ends with two provisions introduced by the word Provided. The first says that no amendment which may be made prior to the year one thousand eight hundred and eight shall in any manner affect the first and fourth clauses in the ninth section of the first article. The second says that no state, without its consent, shall be deprived of its equal suffrage in the Senate.

questions.stem: The source quotes the two provisos. Which three of the following are protected or preserved by them?

options.text: The fourth clause of the ninth section of the first article, until the year the proviso names
The equal suffrage of every state in the Senate, which cannot be taken without that state's consent
The right of the people to keep and bear arms, which no amendment may take away
options.misconception: invents a proviso that the quoted text does not contain

options.text: The first clause of the ninth section of the first article, until the year the proviso names

questions.explanation: Count what the two provisos actually reach. The first proviso names two clauses of the ninth section of the first article, the first and the fourth, and ties its protection to amendments made before a year it names, so the first and second choices are correct. The second proviso protects the equal suffrage of a state in the Senate and requires that state's own consent, so the third choice is correct as well. The fourth choice describes a right that is protected elsewhere in the Constitution but not by either of these provisos, and the quoted text contains no such provision, which is the point of reading the two provisos in full. Each amendment of the last two centuries has been tested against the second proviso, which is what makes it a standing condition on the amendment power rather than a statement of policy.
questions.hint: Read both provisos and list what each one names.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The order of steps in ratifying an amendment
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps by which an amendment becomes part of the Constitution
questions.stem: Four steps stand between a call for an amendment and the amendment's becoming part of the Constitution. Put them in the order Article Five gives, beginning with the step that starts the process.

options.text: An amendment is proposed, by a vote of two-thirds of both houses or by a convention called on the application of the states
Congress proposes the mode of ratification, whether by state legislatures or by state conventions
The states ratify, three-fourths of them in the mode that has been proposed
The amendment becomes valid as part of the Constitution, subject to the two provisos at the end of Article Five

questions.explanation: The order follows the sentence of Article Five. The Congress proposes, either whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary or on the application of the Legislatures of two thirds of the several States, which is the first step because nothing can be ratified before something has been proposed. The choice of mode comes next, because the words as the one or the other Mode of Ratification may be proposed by the Congress make the mode a decision that has to be taken before the states act, and taking it after ratification would leave the states guessing which route they were using. Ratification by three-fourths of the several states in that mode is the third step, and the closing words, that an amendment is valid to all Intents and Purposes as Part of this Constitution when ratified, place the amendment in the Constitution at the fourth step, subject to the provisos that follow.
questions.hint: Work along the single sentence of Article Five from the first verb to the last.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The clause that spent its own force
questions.learningObjective: identify the clause of Article One, Section 9 that ceased to operate by its own terms

stimulus.body: A class table lists the eight clauses of Article One, Section 9. Row 1 concerns the migration or importation of persons and contains a year. Row 2 concerns the writ of habeas corpus. Row 3 concerns bills of attainder and ex post facto laws. Row 4 concerns a capitation or other direct tax. Row 5 concerns articles exported from a state. Row 6 concerns a preference between the ports of one state and another. Row 7 concerns money drawn from the treasury. Row 8 concerns titles of nobility.

questions.stem: Which of the eight rows in the table is the clause that ceased to operate by its own terms rather than remaining in force?

options.text: Row 8, because a title of nobility may no longer be granted by the United States
options.misconception: confuses a prohibition with a provision that has expired

options.text: Row 1, whose protection of the states' power over the importation of persons was limited to the years before the year it names
Row 2, because a writ may be suspended when the public safety requires it
options.misconception: reads a conditional permission as an expiry by its own terms

options.text: Row 7, because money may be drawn only in consequence of appropriations made by law
options.misconception: reads a restriction as a clause that has run out

questions.explanation: Only one of the eight clauses carries a date at which its own operation ends. Row 1 provides that the migration or importation of such persons as the states then existing should think proper to admit shall not be prohibited by the Congress prior to the year one thousand eight hundred and eight, so the bar on Congress lasts only until that year and afterwards the clause has nothing left to do, which is why it is described as having spent its force. The other three answers each pick a clause that still does work: row 2 is conditional and still operates whenever its condition holds, row 7 is a restriction on drawing money that has never lapsed, and row 8 is a prohibition that remains in force precisely because nothing has repealed it. A prohibition and an expiry are opposite things, and telling them apart is the whole distinction in this question.
questions.hint: Look for the only row whose text contains a year at which its own operation stops.

questions.topic: Two senators from each state beside the equal suffrage proviso
questions.learningObjective: connect the representation rule in Article One to the proviso in Article Five
questions.stem: Article One, Section 3 gives each state two senators, and the last proviso of Article Five says no state shall be deprived of its equal suffrage in the Senate without its consent. How do the two provisions fit?

options.text: The proviso guards the arrangement the earlier clause establishes, and it attaches the protection to the state that would be deprived
The proviso replaces the two-senator rule with a rule that lets a state choose how many senators it has
options.misconception: turns a protection of the existing rule into a power to change it

options.text: The proviso applies only where a state is admitted to the Union after the original thirteen
options.misconception: confines the proviso to later admissions, which it does not do

options.text: The proviso is a statement about representation in the House rather than about the Senate
options.misconception: moves the proviso to the chamber it does not mention

questions.explanation: The two provisions do different work on the same subject. Article One, Section 3 opens by providing that the Senate shall be composed of two Senators from each State, and the proviso at the end of Article Five says that no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate. So the earlier clause supplies the arrangement and the proviso protects it, and the proviso's own terms are the only route by which the protection can be lifted, which is why the second answer is wrong: the proviso does not give a state a new power, it withholds one. The third answer invents a limitation to later admissions, and the fourth answer names the wrong chamber. Comparing the two is a quick way to see that equal representation in the Senate is treated differently from representation in the House, which Article One apportions by population.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two provisions supplies the rule and which one protects it.

questions.stem: The compensation clause of Article One, Section 6 says how the amount paid to senators and representatives is arrived at. What does it say?

options.misconception: substitutes a joint resolution of the two houses for a statute

options.text: That the compensation is fixed by the Constitution itself and may not be altered

Two elements: the amount is ascertained by law, and the payment comes from the treasury. The first answer states both. The second answer is the error of substituting a vote of the two houses for the law the clause names, and the third answer moves the determination to the states, which the clause does not do even though the members are chosen in their states. The fourth answer is a confusion with the Twenty-seventh Amendment, which regulates when a law varying the compensation may take effect rather than fixing the amount in the Constitution. questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Rules for the chamber against limits on the chamber
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the clauses that govern Congress's own procedure from those that limit what it may do
questions.stem: Two of the clauses in Article One, Section 9 tell Congress how it must conduct itself, and the others tell Congress what it may not do. Explain the difference between those two kinds of clause, why the difference matters when a measure is challenged, and how the one part of Section 9 that is neither kind fits.

answer.exemplar: Section 9 mixes three different kinds of provision, and the difference between them is the difference between a rule about method and a rule about subject matter. The clauses that tell Congress how to conduct itself require a statement and account of receipts and expenditures to be published from time to time, and they limit the use of titles of nobility, which is a prohibition on what the United States and its officers may do. The clauses that limit what Congress may do forbid a capitation or other direct tax unless it is laid in proportion to the census, forbid a tax or duty on articles exported from a state, forbid a preference between the ports of one state and another, and forbid money to be drawn from the treasury except in consequence of appropriations made by law. A rule about method tells the body how to exercise a power it has, and a rule about subject matter tells the body which subjects are outside the power it has. That is why the two kinds are litigated differently. A challenge to a rule about method usually takes the form of saying that the rule is inconsistent with an express constitutional requirement, such as a command about the journal, and the question is whether the chamber's own enactment can set that requirement aside. A challenge to a rule about subject matter takes the form of saying that the body acted on a subject it has no power to reach, and the question is whether the power claimed can be found in the text at all. The clause about the migration or importation of persons is neither, because it is a limitation on Congress with a date in it, so it constrained Congress for a period and then ceased to operate, and a clause like that is best understood as a rule about what the body may do with an expiry attached rather than as a rule about method. A strong answer therefore sorts the clauses rather than describing Section 9 as a list, and explains that the sort explains which questions a court can reach.

questions.explanation: A strong answer sorts the clauses of Section 9 into method rules and subject matter limits, explains that the two kinds answer different questions and so are tested differently, and places the clause that carries a date with the limits while noting that it has expired. It should not treat the section as a single undifferentiated list.
questions.hint: Ask of each clause whether it tells the body how to act or what it may act on.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The two election intervals compared
questions.learningObjective: compare the interval at which each chamber's membership turns over
questions.stem: Article One says the House is composed of members chosen every second year, and it says one third of the Senate may be chosen every second year. Which comparison is right?

options.text: The House turns over every two years, and the Senate's classes are chosen every fourth year
options.misconception: moves the Senate's interval from two years to four

options.text: The whole House turns over every two years, while a senator serves six years and only one third of the Senate turns over at each election
Both chambers turn over entirely at each election, and the difference is only the length of the term
options.misconception: ignores the three classes that stagger the Senate's elections

options.text: The whole House turns over every six years, and the Senate's three classes are chosen all together
options.misconception: swaps the two terms and puts the Senate's classes in a single election

questions.explanation: The two clauses work differently and the difference is worth stating precisely. The House is composed of members chosen every second Year, so the whole chamber comes up together at an election held every second year, and a representative's term is the same two years. The Senate provides for two senators from each state for six years, and then divides the senators into three classes whose seats are vacated at the expiration of the second year, the fourth year and the sixth year, so that one third may be chosen every second Year. So at any election a third of the Senate is chosen while the rest sit out another term, and the first answer states both intervals and the reason they differ. The second answer treats the Senate as though it were elected as a body, and the last two each move a number the clauses supply.
questions.hint: Find the two terms and then find the sentence that divides the Senate into three classes.
